# Neural surrogates for PDEs: a field guide {#sec-landscape}

*Before this chapter:* @sec-problem, for the boundary-to-field operator, the
interface and the metric. The chapter assumes integral operators,
quadrature, Green's functions and gradient descent on a multilayer
perceptron. It assumes nothing about transformers.

**Every neural surrogate in this book is a composition of a dozen learned
nonlinear integral operators, each applied to a cloud of sampled points.
The families of the literature differ in three choices: how they make the
kernel cheap enough to apply at $10^5$ to $10^7$ points, which symmetries
they build in, and which measure their sums integrate against.** This
chapter teaches the machinery in the vocabulary of numerical analysis:
tokens, attention as a kernel smoother, the transformer block as a product
of near-identity maps, and the families that avoid the quadratic cost of
attention. It then reviews symmetry, discretization and physics-informed
losses, gathers the families into one table, and names the two gaps that
ISLA fills. The terms defined here (token, embedding, attention, softmax,
residual stream, LayerNorm, pre-LN block, MLP) are used in the rest of the
book without redefinition. Citations are by author and year. Full entries,
with arXiv identifiers, are in the bibliography of @sec-vs-bibliography.

```{python}

#| include: false

```

## What a surrogate learns {#sec-landscape-task}

**A surrogate is a parametrized map, fitted to solver output, that stands
in for the solution operator of a family of problems.** A training set is a
few hundred to a few thousand cases. Each case pairs an input (here a
discretized boundary, its data and the global conditions) with the field a
conventional solver computed for it. Training adjusts the parameters
$\theta$ of a map $\mathcal G_\theta$ by stochastic gradient descent on the
mean error over the cases. The trained map is then evaluated on cases it
has not seen. One forward pass costs seconds where the solver costs hours.

Two broad kinds of surrogate exist. A *time stepper* learns the map from
the state at one instant to the state at the next and is applied
recursively, so its errors compound over a rollout. A *solution-operator
surrogate* learns the map from the problem data to the answer in one
evaluation. The steady boundary-driven problems of this book are of the
second kind, and they are a special case in three ways that shape every
architecture choice.

1. **The input lives on a set of one lower dimension than the output.** The
   input is a surface (a curve, in two dimensions) with data on it. The
   output is a field on that surface and in the volume it bounds.
   Green's representation (@eq-green) says this is not a loss of
   information: for the admitted class, the boundary data determine the
   field.
2. **The input is an unordered set of sampled cells of variable size.**
   Two cars have different meshes with different cell counts, and nothing
   about the order in which a mesher lists its cells is physical. An
   architecture must therefore accept a set of $N$ points for any $N$ and
   give an answer that does not depend on their order. This is
   *permutation invariance*.
3. **Every interior point depends on every boundary cell.** The
   representation of @eq-green has no cutoff radius. Any architecture must
   either couple all points directly, at a cost that grows like $N^2$, or
   reach global coupling through a cheaper intermediary.

The rest of this chapter is about the third point and its consequences.

## Tokens, attention and the transformer block {#sec-landscape-transformer}

**A transformer is a map from a set of vectors to a set of vectors of the
same size. It alternates a step that mixes the vectors with one another
(attention) and a step that transforms each vector alone (the MLP), and it
adds each step's output to a running state.** This section defines each
piece once, for the whole book.

### A token is a sampled point with features {#sec-landscape-tokens}

**The network sees each boundary cell as one vector, called a token, and
the whole case as a set of $N$ tokens.** A cell's raw features are whatever
the interface hands over: its position $x_i$, outward normal $n_i$,
measure $w_i$ and its boundary data. In two dimensions that is
five numbers before any boundary data. A learned map, usually a small
multilayer perceptron (MLP), lifts these raw features to a vector
$h_i \in \mathbb R^D$. This vector is the token's *embedding*, or its
*state*, and $D$ is the *width* of the network ($d$ is reserved for the
spatial dimension). The reference
configurations of this book are `{python} S.CONFIG["ISLA"]`,
`{python} S.CONFIG["Transolver"]` and `{python} S.CONFIG["GeoTransolver"]`
(@sec-baselines). The token states of a case form an $N \times D$ array whose row
order carries no meaning (@fig-landscape-tokens).

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-tokens
#| fig-cap: >

#|   airfoil, one of them highlighted with its normal. Middle: that cell's
#|   raw features (position, normal, measure). Right: the token states of all
#|   60 cells after a randomly initialized two-layer embedding to width
#|   D = 32, one row per cell; the highlighted row is the highlighted cell.
#|   How to read this: the embedding here is random, so the colors carry no

H = gelu(feats @ W1) @ W2
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.6, 3.3))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, width_ratios=[2.3, 0.7, 1.15], wspace=0.4)
ax0 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]); ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1]); ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[2])
clean_axes(ax0)

```

A token need not be a boundary cell. An interior prediction point becomes a
token the same way, from its position and whatever geometric features the
architecture computes for it. A latent token, met below, is a vector that
belongs to no point at all.

### Attention is a data-dependent kernel integral {#sec-landscape-attention}

**Attention replaces each token's state with a weighted average of the
values of all the tokens, and the weights form a normalized kernel computed
from the tokens themselves. In the language of statistics it is a
Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoother whose kernel is learned and depends on the
data.** Each token $i$ forms three vectors by fixed linear maps of its
state: a *query* $q_i = W_Q h_i$, a *key* $k_i = W_K h_i$ and a *value*
$v_i = W_V h_i$. Token $i$'s output is

$$
\operatorname{Attn}(h)_i \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{N} \alpha_{ij}\, v_j ,
\qquad
\alpha_{ij} \equiv \frac{\exp\!\bigl(q_i \cdot k_j/\sqrt{d_k}\bigr)}{\sum_{l=1}^{N}\exp\!\bigl(q_i \cdot k_l/\sqrt{d_k}\bigr)},
$$ {#eq-attention}

where $d_k$ is the length of a query. The map from a row of scores
$s_j = q_i \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d_k}$ to the weights $\alpha_{ij}$ is the
*softmax*: it exponentiates and normalizes, so the weights are positive
and sum to one over $j$. The factor $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the scores of
order one when the entries of $q$ and $k$ are of order one (Vaswani et al.,
2017; @sec-vs-bibliography).

Read @eq-attention as quadrature. Let the tokens sample a domain at points
$y_j$ and write the kernel as $\kappa(x, y) = \exp(q(x)\cdot k(y)/\sqrt{d_k})$.
Then attention is the discrete form of the normalized integral operator

$$
(\mathcal A v)(x) = \frac{\int \kappa(x,y)\, v(y)\, d\mu(y)}{\int \kappa(x,y)\, d\mu(y)} ,
$$

with $\mu$ the *empirical measure* $\frac1N\sum_j \delta_{y_j}$, one unit of
mass per token. This is the Nadaraya–Watson estimator of nonparametric
regression (Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964). Tsai et al. (2019) make the
reading explicit for transformers. Three things set it apart from the
smoothers a numerical analyst knows. The kernel is learned, through $W_Q$
and $W_K$. It depends on the current states, so the operator is nonlinear
in its input. And the measure counts tokens, not area; @sec-landscape-discretization
returns to that.

A dot-product kernel can express the Gaussian kernel exactly, which makes
the smoother concrete. Give a token at position $y$ the key
$k = (y/h,\ -y^2/2h^2)$ and a token at $x$ the query $q = (x/h,\ 1)$. Then
$q\cdot k = -(x-y)^2/2h^2 + x^2/2h^2$, and the last term is the same for
every $j$, so the softmax cancels it. What remains is the Gaussian kernel of
bandwidth $h$. Append the same construction for a field value $f$ carried
in the state, and the kernel becomes
$\exp(-(x-y)^2/2h^2 - (f(x)-f(y))^2/2s^2)$. That is the bilateral filter
of image processing: it averages over neighbors that are close in position
*and* in value, so it does not smear a jump. @fig-landscape-attention
computes both on a one-dimensional signal.

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-attention
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Attention as a kernel smoother, computed exactly with the dot-product
#|   construction of the text on noisy samples of a signal with a jump,
#|   drawn more densely on the left (160 samples, noise 0.06). Top: the samples (gray), the noise-free
#|   signal (thin gray line), the output of attention whose keys and queries
#|   carry position only (dashed, a Gaussian Nadaraya–Watson smoother of
#|   bandwidth 0.05), and the output when they also carry the sampled value
#|   (violet, a bilateral filter); the window from 0.25 to 0.85 is shown. Bottom: the attention weights of one
#|   query, the token at x = 0.53 just left of the jump, under each kernel.
#|   How to read this: the position-only weights spill across the jump and
#|   pull the output toward the far side; the value-dependent weights stay on
#|   one side. Nothing here is trained: the queries and keys are constructed
#|   by hand to show what the formula can represent.
#| fig-height: 5.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
N1 = 160
x1 = np.sort(rng.random(N1) ** 1.3)
f_true = lambda x: 0.45 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * x) + 0.8 * (x > 0.55)
f1 = f_true(x1) + rng.normal(0, 0.06, N1)
hh, ss = 0.05, 0.3
def attn(q, k, v):
    s = q @ k.T
    s -= s.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    a = np.exp(s); a /= a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return a @ v, a
q_pos = np.column_stack([x1 / hh, np.ones(N1)]); k_pos = np.column_stack([x1 / hh, -x1**2 / (2 * hh**2)])
q_val = np.column_stack([q_pos, f1 / ss, np.ones(N1)]); k_val = np.column_stack([k_pos, f1 / ss, -f1**2 / (2 * ss**2)])
y_pos, A_pos = attn(q_pos, k_pos, f1)
y_val, A_val = attn(q_val, k_val, f1)
iq = np.argmin(np.abs(x1 - 0.53))
fig, (a0, a1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.5, 1]))
xx = np.linspace(0, 1, 800)
a0.plot(xx, f_true(xx), color=BASELINE, lw=1.0)
a0.plot(x1, f1, "o", ms=3, color=MUTED, alpha=0.7)
a0.plot(x1, y_pos, color=INK2, lw=1.8, ls="--")
a0.plot(x1, y_val, color=VIOLET, lw=2.0)
a0.axvline(x1[iq], color=AQUA, lw=1.0, ls=":")
label_line(a0, 0.585, 0.05, "position-only kernel\n(Nadaraya–Watson)", INK2, fontsize=8.5)
label_line(a0, 0.40, 0.72, "position and value\n(bilateral filter)", VIOLET, fontsize=8.5)
a0.set_ylabel("signal $f$ [–]")
a0.set_title("attention output for every token")
a1.vlines(x1 - 0.002, 0, A_pos[iq], color=INK2, lw=1.6)
a1.vlines(x1 + 0.002, 0, A_val[iq], color=VIOLET, lw=1.6)
a1.axvline(0.55, color=BASELINE, lw=1.0)
a1.text(0.555, A_val[iq].max() * 0.92, "jump", color=MUTED, fontsize=8.5)
a1.axvline(x1[iq], color=AQUA, lw=1.0, ls=":")
a1.text(x1[iq] - 0.01, A_val[iq].max() * 0.92, "query", color=AQUA, fontsize=8.5, ha="right")
a1.set_xlim(0.25, 0.85); a1.set_ylim(0, None)
a1.set_xlabel("position of token $j$ [–]"); a1.set_ylabel(r"weight $\alpha_{ij}$ [–]")
a1.set_title("the weights of one query")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A transformer runs several attentions side by side. *Multi-head attention*
splits the $D$ features into $H$ groups of $D/H$, runs @eq-attention on
each group with its own $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, and concatenates the results.
Each head is a different kernel. The step costs one score per pair of
tokens and per head: an $N \times N$ array, which is the subject of
@sec-landscape-cost.

### The block: residual stream, LayerNorm and the MLP {#sec-landscape-block}

**A transformer block adds two small updates to a running state: one that
mixes tokens (attention) and one that transforms each token alone (the
MLP). Each update reads a normalized copy of the state. The network is
therefore a product of near-identity maps, like the steps of an explicit
time integrator.** @fig-landscape-block draws one block.

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-block
#| fig-cap: >
#|   One pre-LN transformer block. The residual stream (the thick line) carries
#|   the token states from left to right. Each of the two branches reads a
#|   LayerNorm of the stream, computes an update, and adds it back at a
#|   circled plus. Attention couples the tokens; the MLP acts on each token
#|   separately. Blue boxes are learned maps; the dashed white boxes are
#|   normalizations with only a per-feature scale and shift to learn. How to
#|   read this: the stream itself is never normalized or overwritten inside the
#|   block, only added to; a stack of L blocks is the same picture repeated L
#|   times.
#| fig-height: 2.6
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.4, 2.6))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 2.5); ax.axis("off")
ax.annotate("", xy=(9.9, 0.3), xytext=(0.1, 0.3), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=3.0))
ax.text(0.15, 0.0, r"stream $h^{(\ell)}$", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
ax.text(9.85, 0.0, r"$h^{(\ell+1)}$", fontsize=9.5, color=INK, ha="right")
def box(x, y, wdt, txt, learned):
    fc, ec, ls = ("#e6f0fb", BLUE, "-") if learned else (WHITE, BLUE, (0, (4, 3)))
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y), wdt, 0.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.04", fc=fc, ec=ec, ls=ls, lw=1.4))
    ax.text(x + wdt / 2, y + 0.3, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
def plus(x):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((x, 0.3), 0.17, fc=WHITE, ec=INK, lw=1.4, zorder=5))
    ax.text(x, 0.3, "+", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, zorder=6)
for x0, name, xp in ((1.0, "attention\n(mixes tokens)", 4.6), (5.4, "MLP\n(per token)", 9.0)):
    ax.plot([x0, x0], [0.3, 1.5], color=INK2, lw=1.4)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 0.16, 1.5), xytext=(x0, 1.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK2, lw=1.4))
    box(x0 + 0.2, 1.2, 0.85, "LN", False)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 1.55, 1.5), xytext=(x0 + 1.05, 1.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK2, lw=1.4))
    box(x0 + 1.6, 1.2, 1.7, name, True)
    ax.plot([x0 + 3.3, xp], [1.5, 1.5], color=INK2, lw=1.4)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(xp, 0.5), xytext=(xp, 1.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK2, lw=1.4))
    plus(xp)
plt.show()
```

The *residual stream* is the sequence of token states $h^{(0)}, h^{(1)},
\dots, h^{(L)}$ that passes through the $L$ blocks. A block never replaces
it. It adds to it:

$$
h \leftarrow h + \operatorname{Attn}\bigl(\operatorname{LN}(h)\bigr),
\qquad
h \leftarrow h + \operatorname{MLP}\bigl(\operatorname{LN}(h)\bigr).
$$ {#eq-preln}

*LayerNorm* (LN) normalizes each token separately across its $D$ features:
it subtracts the token's feature mean, divides by the token's feature
standard deviation, and applies a learned per-feature scale $\gamma$ and
shift $\beta$ (Ba et al., 2016). So
$\operatorname{LN}(h)_i = \gamma \odot (h_i - \bar h_i)/\operatorname{std}(h_i) + \beta$,
whatever the size of $h_i$. The *MLP* is a two-layer perceptron applied to
each token alone, $\operatorname{MLP}(u) = W_2\,\phi(W_1 u)$, with a hidden
width of four times $D$ and a smooth rectifier $\phi$, usually the GELU
(Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016). Attention is the only step that couples
tokens. The block is the pattern of a neural-operator layer,
$\sigma(Wv + \mathcal K v)$ (Kovachki et al., 2023): a nonlocal integral
operator, then a pointwise nonlinearity.

**Each block is a near-identity map.** When its updates are small against
the stream, a block's Jacobian is $I + O(\varepsilon)$ and the network is a
product $\prod_\ell (I + F_\ell)$ of perturbations of the identity. This is
forward Euler on $\dot h = F(h, t)$ (Haber and Ruthotto, 2017), and it is
why very deep residual networks train at all (He et al., 2016): the
gradient reaches the first layer through the identity path. The arrangement
of @eq-preln is the *pre-LN block* (Xiong et al., 2020). It is
called pre-LN because the normalization sits before each sublayer, inside
the branch. The original transformer normalized after the addition, which
needs a learning-rate *warm-up*, a rate raised gradually from near zero over
the first steps, to train.

The argument for why every branch reads the normalized state, and why ISLA's
slice sublayer does too, is in @sec-isla-normalized-reads.

Other placements of the normalization exist. The *sandwich* or *peri-LN*
block also normalizes each sublayer's output before the addition (Ding et
al., 2021; Kim et al., 2025). *QK-normalization* normalizes queries and keys
before the dot product, which bounds every score (Henry et al., 2020;
Dehghani et al., 2023). The *normalized transformer* keeps every state on
the unit sphere (Loshchilov et al., 2024). All of them control the scale of
what a sublayer reads, and that is the property that matters here.

## Why $N^2$ is impossible at 200,000 points, and the ways around it {#sec-landscape-cost}

**Dense attention scores every pair of tokens. At the 200,000 cells per
case of this book's protocol, the score arrays of one layer fill several
GPUs, and their arithmetic costs GPU-days per training run. Every scalable family replaces the dense $N \times N$ kernel with
something of cost linear in $N$, or $N \log N$ for a tree code.** The arithmetic, for a network of the
width and depth of ISLA:

```{python}
#| label: para-landscape-cost
#| output: asis
N, d, Hh, L, M = 200_000, 512, 8, 12, 512   # d here is the width D of the text
DRV_CELLS = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "problem_figures_2026-09-22" / "drivaer.json"))["n_surface_cells"]
GiB = 2**30
score_one = N * N * 2 / GiB                # one head, one layer, bfloat16 (2 bytes)
score_all = score_one * Hh
fl_attn = 4 * N * N * d                    # QK^T and AV, 2 flops per multiply-add each
fl_mlp = 16 * N * d * d                    # two matmuls d -> 4d -> d
fl_slice = 6 * N * M * d                   # routing logits, pooling and read-back, N x M x d each
thr = 4e14                                 # assumed sustained arithmetic rate, FLOP/s
steps = 1e5
t_step = 3 * L * fl_attn / thr             # forward + backward ~ 3x forward
def sci(x):
    e = int(np.floor(np.log10(x))); return f"{x / 10**e:.1f} \\times 10^{{{e}}}"
print(f"- one $N \\times N$ score array, one head, one layer, in bfloat16: ${score_one:.0f}$ GiB; "
      f"all {Hh} heads of one layer: ${score_all:.0f}$ GiB, against 80 GiB on one GPU;\n"
      f"- arithmetic of dense attention per layer, forward: ${sci(fl_attn)}$ floating-point operations, "
      f"{fl_attn / fl_mlp:.0f} times the MLP's ${sci(fl_mlp)}$;\n"
      f"- a training step of {L} layers (backward about twice the forward): "
      f"{t_step:.1f} s of attention arithmetic alone at an assumed sustained ${sci(thr)}$ FLOP/s, "
      f"so {steps * t_step / 86400:.0f} GPU-days for $10^5$ steps;\n"
      f"- slice attention with $M = {M}$ slices instead: ${sci(fl_slice)}$ per layer, "
      f"{fl_attn / fl_slice:.0f} times less than dense attention and below the MLP.\n\n"
      f"Memory-efficient attention kernels (Dao et al., 2022) never store the score array, which removes the "
      f"first line; they leave the arithmetic unchanged. At $10^7$ points, the order of a full DrivAerML "
      f"surface mesh (the car drawn in @fig-datasets has {DRV_CELLS:,} cells), the arithmetic is "
      f"{(1e7 / N) ** 2:,.0f} times larger. The rate ${sci(thr)}$ FLOP/s is an assumption of this worked "
      f"example, not a measurement.")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-cost

a1.set_xlabel("tokens per case $N$ [–]")

for a in (a0, a1):

a0.set_yticks([1e-2, 1, 1e2, 1e4, 1e6]); a0.set_yticklabels(["0.01", "1", "100", "10,000", "1,000,000"])
```

**Four families route the global coupling through something cheaper.**
@fig-landscape-routes draws them on the airfoil. A numerical analyst knows
each one already: a stencil, a spectral method on a background grid, a
coarse basis, and an algebraic coarse level.

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-routes
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Four ways to couple N boundary tokens at a cost linear in N, drawn on the
#|   running airfoil (60 cells). (a) Local neighborhoods: each token exchanges
#|   messages with its nearest neighbors; after three rounds the highlighted
#|   token has reached the shaded ones. (b) A regular latent grid: tokens
#|   are scattered onto grid nodes, a spectral convolution acts on the grid,
#|   and the result is gathered back. (c) Learned latent tokens: a fixed set
#|   of M vectors (squares) cross-attends to every token; each line is one
#|   attention weight of one latent token. (d) Slice attention: a soft
#|   partition of the tokens into M slices, one slice state per color. How to
#|   read this: the figure shows the coupling pattern of each family, not any
#|   trained weights; M = 6 here, a few hundred in practice.
#| fig-height: 4.6
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.6))
P = mid; Nn = len(P)
for ax in axs.flat:
    clean_axes(ax); ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.0)
    ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.15, 1.45)
# (a) graph: ring neighbors (k = 2 each side), three hops
ax = axs[0, 0]; i0 = 15
for i in range(Nn):
    for o in (1, 2):
        j = (i + o) % Nn
        ax.plot(P[[i, j], 0], P[[i, j], 1], color=GRID, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
reach = {(i0 + o) % Nn for o in range(-6, 7)}
ax.plot(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], "o", ms=3, color=INK2, zorder=2)
ax.plot(P[list(reach), 0], P[list(reach), 1], "o", ms=6, color=VIOLET, alpha=0.35, zorder=2)
ax.plot(P[i0, 0], P[i0, 1], "o", ms=7, color=VIOLET, zorder=3)
ax.set_title("(a) local neighborhoods: graph networks")
# (b) latent grid
ax = axs[0, 1]
gx = np.linspace(-2.3, 2.3, 12); gy = np.linspace(-1.1, 1.3, 7)
for xg in gx: ax.plot([xg, xg], [gy[0], gy[-1]], color=GRID, lw=0.8)
for yg in gy: ax.plot([gx[0], gx[-1]], [yg, yg], color=GRID, lw=0.8)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(gx, gy); ax.plot(GX, GY, "s", ms=3, color=VIOLET, alpha=0.7)

    ax.plot([P[i, 0], gx[jx]], [P[i, 1], gy[jy]], color=VIOLET, lw=0.8)
ax.set_title("(b) a latent grid: FNO, Geo-FNO, GINO")
# (c) latent tokens
ax = axs[1, 0]
lat = np.column_stack([np.linspace(-2.0, 2.0, 6), np.full(6, 1.32)])
ax.plot(lat[:, 0], lat[:, 1], "s", ms=8, color=VIOLET)

for m in (1, 4):
    sc = -np.sum((P - (lat[m] - [0, 1.3])) ** 2, 1) / 0.6
    wts = np.exp(sc - sc.max()); wts /= wts.max()
    for i in range(Nn):
        ax.plot([P[i, 0], lat[m, 0]], [P[i, 1], lat[m, 1]], color=VIOLET, lw=0.4 + 1.2 * wts[i], alpha=0.15 + 0.6 * wts[i])
ax.set_title("(c) latent tokens: Perceiver, UPT, AB-UPT")
# (d) slices
ax = axs[1, 1]
cent = np.array([[-1.9, 0.05], [-1.1, 0.35], [-0.1, 0.45], [0.9, 0.25], [1.8, 0.0], [0.0, -0.1]])
lg = -np.sum((P[:, None, :] - cent[None]) ** 2, -1) / 0.25
Wsl = np.exp(lg - lg.max(1, keepdims=True)); Wsl /= Wsl.sum(1, keepdims=True)
cols = slice_colors(6, seed=3)
rgba = Wsl @ cols[:, :3]
ax.scatter(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], s=28, c=np.clip(rgba, 0, 1), edgecolor="none", zorder=3)

```

### Local neighborhoods: graph networks {#sec-landscape-graph}

**A graph network replaces the global kernel with a stencil and recovers
global coupling by applying it many times.** MeshGraphNets treats the
simulation mesh as a graph (Pfaff et al., 2021; @sec-vs-bibliography). Each
layer computes a message on every edge from the two endpoint states and
their relative position, sums the incoming messages at every node, and
updates the node state with an MLP. A layer costs $O(Nk)$ for $k$
neighbors per node. A message travels one edge per layer, so a signal
crosses a mesh of diameter $D$ edges only after $D$ layers. Elliptic
problems couple everything, so a purely local network needs very many
layers or a hierarchy of coarsened graphs, as a multigrid solver does.
Message-passing PDE solvers (Brandstetter et al., 2022) show that this class
contains finite differences and finite volumes as special cases. The sum
over neighbors weights each neighbor once, whatever the size of its cell.

### Spectral and latent grids: FNO, Geo-FNO, GINO {#sec-landscape-grid}

**A Fourier neural operator writes the kernel integral as a convolution on
a regular grid and applies it with the FFT, truncated to a few modes.**
The *neural operator* framework (Kovachki et al., 2023) defines each layer
as $v \mapsto \sigma(Wv + \mathcal K v)$, with $\mathcal K$ an integral
operator with a learned kernel, and asks that the layers converge as the
discretization is refined. The graph kernel network (Li et al., 2020)
evaluates $\mathcal K$ as a quadrature sum over a radius graph. The FNO
(Li et al., 2021) takes $\kappa(x,y)=\kappa(x-y)$ and multiplies Fourier
coefficients by learned matrices, at cost $O(n \log n)$ on $n$ grid nodes.
An irregular geometry must first be put on a grid. Geo-FNO learns a deformation of the
physical domain onto a uniform latent grid (Li et al., 2023a). GINO reads the shape as a point cloud and a signed-distance
function, uses a graph neural operator to carry features onto a regular
latent grid, applies an FNO there, and maps the result back to
arbitrary query points (Li et al., 2023b). The
grid is a background mesh, and its resolution, not the number of input
points, sets the cost and the smallest resolved scale: a thin boundary
layer on a car needs a fine grid in a large box.

### Learned latent tokens: Perceiver, UPT, AB-UPT {#sec-landscape-latent}

**A latent-token model compresses the $N$ inputs into $M \ll N$ learned
vectors by cross-attention, processes those, and decodes at any query
point.** *Cross-attention* is @eq-attention with the queries from one set
of tokens and the keys and values from another. The Perceiver keeps a fixed
array of $M$ latent vectors as queries and attends from them to the $N$
inputs, at cost $NM$, then runs ordinary attention among the latents, at
cost $M^2$ (Jaegle et al., 2021). Perceiver IO decodes by a second
cross-attention from output queries to the latents (Jaegle et al., 2022).
The latent array is a learned coarse basis: the encoder is a projection
onto it and the decoder an interpolation from it. Universal Physics
Transformers (UPT) encode a mesh or particle set into a latent set,
propagate it there and query the latent field at arbitrary points (Alkin et
al., 2024). AB-UPT, its automotive form, runs attention on a reduced set of
*anchor* tokens drawn from the points, uses separate branches for the
geometry, the surface and the volume, and lets the remaining query points
cross-attend to the anchors (Alkin et al., 2025). It reports volume meshes
up to 150 million cells, and it predicts the vorticity as the curl of a
learned field, so the predicted vorticity is divergence-free by
construction.

### Slice attention: Transolver {#sec-landscape-slice}

**Slice attention routes each token softly into $M$ slices, runs attention
among the $M$ slice states, and spreads the result back. It factors the
dense $N \times N$ operator through a learned soft partition of unity, the
restriction and prolongation pair of algebraic multigrid.** Transolver
(Wu et al., 2024) computes, for every token, weights over the slices,
$a_{is} = \operatorname{softmax}_s(\text{linear}(h_i)/\tau)$. The softmax
runs over slices, so each token's weights sum to one: the $a_{is}$ form a
partition of unity on the tokens. A slice state is the weighted mean of its
tokens, $Z_s = \sum_i a_{is} h_i / \sum_i a_{is}$. Attention runs among the
$M$ slice states. Token $i$ reads back $\sum_s a_{is} Z'_s$. Written as
matrices, with $P \equiv (a_{is})$ of size $N \times M$ and
$R \equiv \operatorname{diag}(P^\top \mathbf 1)^{-1} P^\top$ of size
$M \times N$, the token-mixing step is

$$
h' = P \, \mathcal A_M \, R \, h ,
$$ {#eq-slice-factor}

with $\mathcal A_M$ the attention among slices. $R$ restricts the fine
level to $M$ coarse unknowns by weighted averages. $P$ prolongs back by a
partition of unity. The fine-level coupling has rank at most $M$, as a
two-level method's coarse correction does (@fig-landscape-slices). The analogy has limits that
matter. The partition is learned, recomputed from the current states in
every layer, and soft. The coarse operator is a nonlinear attention, not a
Galerkin product $R A P$. And the slices group tokens by similarity of
state, which places points of similar physics in one slice wherever they
sit on the body. Hu et al. (2026) show the
mechanism is a form of *linear attention* (attention whose kernel factors
through a feature map, so its cost is linear in $N$), and argue that most of its value
lies in the restriction and prolongation rather than in the attention
among slices. The cost is $O(NMD)$ per layer, which is the line of
@fig-landscape-cost.

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-slices
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Slice attention as a low-rank factorization, on the running airfoil with
#|   M = 6 slices from a hand-made routing (a softmax over slices of the
#|   squared distance to six points). Top: each cell drawn in the blend of
#|   its slices' colors, and each slice's weighted-mean position (stars).
#|   Bottom: the matrices of @eq-slice-factor, drawn to scale: prolongation
#|   P (N × M), the coarse operator A among slices (M × M, here a random
#|   attention), the restriction R (M × N), and their product, an N × N
#|   operator of rank 6. Darker is larger.
#|   How to read this: in a trained network the routing comes from the token
#|   states, not from position, and is recomputed in every layer; this figure
#|   shows only the algebra.
#| fig-height: 5.4
Pm = Wsl                                   # N x M, rows sum to one
Rm = (Pm / Pm.sum(0, keepdims=True)).T     # M x N, rows sum to one
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
sc = rng.normal(0, 1.2, (6, 6)); Am = np.exp(sc); Am /= Am.sum(1, keepdims=True)
K = Pm @ Am @ Rm
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8.6, 5.4))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 7, height_ratios=[0.8, 1.2], width_ratios=[6, 5, 6, 5, 60, 5, 60], hspace=0.12, wspace=0.05)
ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :]); clean_axes(ax)
ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.0)
ax.scatter(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], s=40, c=np.clip(Wsl @ cols[:, :3], 0, 1), edgecolor="none", zorder=3)
zs = Rm @ P
for s in range(6):
    ax.plot(zs[s, 0], zs[s, 1], "*", ms=14, color=cols[s], mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=4)
ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 0.85)
ax.set_title("a soft partition of 60 tokens into 6 slices; stars: slice mean positions")
def mat(axm, Mx, title, cmap="Greys"):
    axm.imshow(Mx, aspect="equal", cmap=cmap, interpolation="nearest", vmin=0)
    axm.set_xticks([]); axm.set_yticks([]); axm.grid(False); axm.set_title(title, fontsize=9, loc="center")
    for sp in axm.spines.values(): sp.set_visible(True); sp.set_color(BASELINE)
mat(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0]), Pm, "P\nN × M")
mat(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2]), Am, "A\nM × M")
mat(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 4]), Rm, "R,  M × N")
mat(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 6]), K, "P · A · R  (N × N, rank 6)")
for k, sym in ((1, "·"), (3, "·"), (5, "=")):
    a_ = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, k]); a_.axis("off"); a_.text(0.5, 0.5, sym, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=18, color=INK)
plt.show()
```

### GeoTransolver and Transolver++ {#sec-landscape-geotransolver}

**GeoTransolver adds a geometry encoder and global context to Transolver;
Transolver++ sharpens the routing and scales it across GPUs.** GeoTransolver
(Adams et al., 2025) pairs the slice self-attention of each block with a
cross-attention to a shared embedding of the geometry and the global
parameters. It computes that embedding once from multi-scale ball queries
(neighborhoods of several radii around each point), after DoMINO (Ranade et
al., 2025), and reuses it in every block. Its configurations in this book
are described in @sec-baselines. Transolver++ (Luo et al., 2025) gives each
point an adaptive routing temperature and samples the slice weights with a
*Gumbel-softmax* (a softmax of logits perturbed by Gumbel noise, a
differentiable stand-in for sampling one slice), against slice weights that
become uniform, and adds a
parallel implementation that reaches million-point meshes. Transolver-3
(Zhou et al., 2026) tiles the slice computation and reorders its matrix
products to reach meshes of over 160 million cells. Transolver and GeoTransolver,
as released in PhysicsNeMo, take each point's raw coordinates along the
dataset's axes and weight each token once in their slice states.

### A learned boundary integral on a tree: GLOBE {#sec-landscape-globe}

**GLOBE takes Green's representation as its architecture: the field at a
target is a sum over the boundary faces of a learned kernel from each face
to the target, weighted by the face's area. It keeps every face-to-target
pair and makes the sum cheap the way an N-body code does, with a
Barnes–Hut tree.** The four families above route the coupling through an
intermediary. GLOBE (Sharpe, 2025) keeps the all-to-all sum of a
boundary-element method and learns its kernel: Green's representation
(@eq-green) with the fundamental solution replaced by a network. For faces
$s$ with centroid $x_s$, normal $n_s$ and area $w_s$ (in units of a
reference area), one evaluation at a target $x_t$ is

$$
\mathcal K_t = \sum_{s=1}^{N} \lambda_s\, w_s\, g\bigl(\lVert r_{ts}\rVert\bigr)\, \kappa(\xi_{ts}),
\qquad
r_{ts} \equiv \frac{x_t - x_s}{\ell},
\qquad
g(r) \equiv \frac{1 - e^{-r^2}}{(1 + r^2)^{(d-1)/2}} ,
$$ {#eq-landscape-globe}

with $\ell$ a reference length of the problem and $\lambda_s$ a learned
strength of the face. The pair's invariants $\xi_{ts}$ are the magnitudes
of its vectors ($r_{ts}$, $n_s$, vector boundary data and latent
vectors) and Legendre polynomials of the cosine between every two of them.
A small network $\kappa$, a ratio of two MLPs shaped like a Padé
approximant, maps them to output channels. A scalar output is one channel.
A vector output is a combination, with coefficients from $\kappa$, of the
pair's own directions: $\hat r_{ts}$, each input vector and its part
orthogonal to $\hat r_{ts}$. The envelope $g$ vanishes at
$r = 0$ and decays like $r^{1-d}$, as the field $\nabla G$ of a point
source does. No softmax normalizes the sum, so it is linear in the
strengths, as @eq-green is linear in the boundary data.

A *communication hyperlayer* evaluates @eq-landscape-globe from the faces
to the faces themselves and returns each face's strengths and latent
fields for the next one, a learned stand-in for the dense solve that gives
a boundary-element method its source densities. By default the class
stacks `{python} GLOBE_DEFAULTS["n_communication_hyperlayers"]` of them
before a last hyperlayer, which evaluates at the requested points,
wherever they lie. Each hyperlayer sums one kernel per reference length and per
boundary-condition type. The kernels are small: the paper's AirfRANS model
has 117,282 parameters.

The decay envelope is what lets a tree code apply. Evaluated densely, a
hyperlayer costs $N^2$ kernel evaluations. A distant cluster of faces
contributes like $r^{1-d}$, so GLOBE's PhysicsNeMo code reads it as one
virtual face: the kernel is evaluated once, at the cluster's area-weighted
centroid with its area-weighted mean normal and data, and multiplied by
the cluster's total $\sum_s \lambda_s w_s$. This is the monopole term of a
multipole expansion, the tree code of Barnes and Hut (1986) and the lowest
order of the fast multipole method. The tree bisects the face centroids
along a Morton space-filling curve. A pair of boxes counts as far when the
sum of their diagonals is below $\theta$ times their gap
($\theta$ is `{python} GLOBE_DEFAULTS["theta"]` by default),
nearer faces are summed one by one, and the cost falls to $O(N \log N)$.
@fig-isla-dtt draws this access pattern on the airfoil. The boxes are
aligned with the dataset's axes, not with the body. At a finite $\theta$ a rotation
therefore regroups the clusters, and the kernel's exact equivariance holds
only to the accuracy of the monopole; at $\theta = 0$ the sum is exact.

ISLA draws on the best parts of GLOBE and of Transolver. From GLOBE it
takes the boundary as the input, the rigid-motion symmetry built into the
architecture exactly, sums over the boundary weighted by the cells'
measure, and dimensionless geometry, in units of a length ISLA computes
from the boundary where GLOBE is given its reference lengths. From
Transolver it takes the coupling: a learned soft partition into slices,
at a cost linear in $N$, in place of GLOBE's kernel per face–target pair
(@sec-landscape-gaps). ISLA-DTT's read-only prediction points follow GLOBE's evaluation
pattern: after every layer each point reads every boundary cell through a
learned kernel of the pair's relative geometry, walking a forest of
GLOBE's cluster trees, near cells one by one and distant clusters as monopoles
(@sec-arch-tree-read). That read is a softmax over the cells with a
log-measure bias, a normalized quadrature, and its forest is built in a
frame the boundary carries, so a rotation does not regroup it, up to ties
of that frame.

### DeepONet: a branch and a trunk {#sec-landscape-deeponet}

**DeepONet writes the solution as a separated expansion: coefficients that
depend on the input function, times basis functions of the query point.**
Its prediction at a point $y$ is $\mathcal G(u)(y) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{p}
b_k(u)\, t_k(y)$ (Lu et al., 2021). A *branch* network maps the input
function, sampled at fixed sensor points, to the coefficients $b_k$. A
*trunk* network maps the query point to the basis values $t_k$. The form
is that of a proper orthogonal decomposition with a learned basis. It
follows a universal approximation theorem for operators (Chen and Chen,
1995). Each query point is evaluated independently of the others, so the
answer at a point does not depend on which other points were requested.
The branch needs the input at fixed sensors, which a varying boundary mesh
does not supply without interpolation.

## Symmetry: augment, canonicalize or build it in {#sec-landscape-symmetry}

**A surrogate can respect a rigid motion in three ways: learn it from
rotated copies of the data, rotate every input to a standard pose first, or
use only operations that commute with the motion. Only the last is exact
for every input, and it constrains the architecture.** The physics of
@sec-problem does not depend on where the body sits or how it is turned
relative to the dataset's axes, so a
correct surrogate satisfies $\mathcal G(Qx + b) = Q\,\mathcal G(x)$ for
vector outputs and $\mathcal G(Qx + b) = \mathcal G(x)$ for scalar outputs,
for every rotation $Q$ and translation $b$, with the normals and the global
directions rotated by $Q$ as well. A map with this property is
*equivariant*, or *invariant* for scalars.

**Data augmentation** trains on randomly rotated and translated copies of
each case. It changes nothing in the architecture, costs training time, and
yields an approximate symmetry only over the poses it was shown. Rygiel et
al. (2026) measure the effect on ShapeNet-Car. Their measure is the median relative L2
error of velocity over five runs. An AB-UPT trained without rotations
scores 1.31% in the training pose and 10.5% at a test rotation of 5°.
Trained on rotations up to 90°, it scores about 2.1% at every test
rotation up to 90° and 10.7% at 180°. The equivariant model of the same
study scores 2.19% at every rotation.

**Canonicalization** maps every input to a standard pose before the
network sees it, for instance by centering on the centroid and aligning the
principal axes of the shape's second moment. The network can then be
anything. The canonical pose is exact where it is unique, and it is
discontinuous where it is not. When two principal moments are nearly
equal, a small change of shape turns the canonical frame through nearly
90°, and when they are equal the turn is a jump (@fig-landscape-canon). Eigenvector signs are a
second ambiguity. Frame averaging averages the network over all the frames
the ambiguity allows (Puny et al., 2022). A learned canonicalizer replaces
the principal axes with a small equivariant network (Kaba et al., 2023).

```{python}
#| label: fig-landscape-canon
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Why a canonical frame is discontinuous. A family of closed curves, an
#|   ellipse with aspect ratio between 0.8 and 1.25 carrying a small
#|   off-axis bump, aligned by the principal axes of its length-weighted
#|   second moment. Top: three members of the family, 3% apart in aspect
#|   ratio, with their first principal axis (a line: an axis has no sign).
#|   Bottom: the angle between that axis and the horizontal, against the
#|   aspect ratio. How to read this: the frame turns through
#|   nearly 90° across a few percent of aspect ratio, where the two principal
#|   moments nearly cross, so a network fed canonical coordinates sees three
#|   near-identical shapes in three different poses; for a shape with an
#|   exact symmetry the turn becomes a jump.
#| fig-height: 5.0
def shape(ar, n=400):
    t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n, endpoint=False)
    r = 1 + 0.03 * np.exp(-((t - 0.8) / 0.25) ** 2)
    pts = np.column_stack([ar * r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)])
    return pts
def axis_angle(pts):
    seg = np.roll(pts, -1, 0) - pts; wl = np.linalg.norm(seg, axis=1); m = pts + seg / 2
    c0 = (wl[:, None] * m).sum(0) / wl.sum(); X = m - c0
    C = (wl[:, None, None] * X[:, :, None] * X[:, None, :]).sum(0)
    ev, V = np.linalg.eigh(C); v = V[:, -1]
    ang = np.degrees(np.arctan2(v[1], v[0])) % 180
    return min(ang, 180 - ang), c0, v
ars = np.linspace(0.8, 1.25, 400)
angs = np.array([axis_angle(shape(a))[0] for a in ars])
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5.0))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3, height_ratios=[1, 1.1], hspace=0.35)
for k, a in enumerate((0.97, 1.0, 1.03)):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, k]); clean_axes(ax)
    pts = shape(a); ang, c0, v = axis_angle(pts)
    ax.plot(*np.vstack([pts, pts[:1]]).T, color=INK, lw=1.5)
    ax.plot(*np.column_stack([c0 - 1.1 * v, c0 + 1.1 * v]), color=VIOLET, lw=1.8)
    ax.set_title(f"aspect ratio {a:.3f}", loc="center", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.5, 1.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.5)
ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :])
ax.plot(ars, angs, color=VIOLET, lw=2.0)
ax.set_xlabel("aspect ratio of the curve [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("first principal axis,\nangle to horizontal [deg]")
ax.set_yticks([0, 45, 90]); ax.set_ylim(-5, 95)
plt.show()
```

**Equivariance by construction** uses only operations that commute with
the group. EGNN builds its messages from relative distances and updates
positions by weighted sums of relative vectors, which is exact for
rotations, translations and reflections at the cost of an MLP on scalars
(Satorras et al., 2021). Tensor field networks and the e3nn library carry
features as irreducible representations of the rotation group (scalars,
vectors, and higher-order tensors written in spherical harmonics) and
combine them with Clebsch–Gordan tensor products (Thomas et al., 2018;
Geiger and Smidt, 2022). The SE(3)-Transformer brings that construction to
attention (Fuchs et al., 2020). The Geometric Algebra Transformer represents
every state as an element of the projective geometric algebra of
three-dimensional space (Brehmer et al., 2023). These networks are exact for
every input. Their price is in every layer: typed features, constrained
linear maps and tensor products whose cost rises steeply with the highest
order carried. In the Rygiel et al. (2026) study, the equivariant AB-GATr
trains 2 to 11 times slower than AB-UPT.

A fourth route sits between the second and the third. Compute the
invariants of the input first (distances, angles, dot products against
vectors that move with the body), run an ordinary network on those scalars,
and rebuild vector outputs at the end from a basis that rotates with the
body. It is exact, it puts the cost at the edges of the network rather than
in every layer, and it is the route ISLA takes (@sec-isla-frame,
@sec-isla-heads). GLOBE takes it inside every kernel evaluation: invariants
of the face–target pair in, vector outputs rebuilt on true vectors of the
pair, which makes it exact under reflections too, for scalar and vector
outputs (Sharpe, 2025).

| route | exact for every input | what it costs | where the cost sits |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| data augmentation | no, approximate over the poses trained | training time and data | in training |
| canonicalization | yes where the frame is unique; discontinuous where it is not | a frame rule and its failure set | at the input |
| equivariant layers (EGNN, e3nn, GATr) | yes | typed features, constrained maps, tensor products | in every layer |
| invariants in, equivariant basis out | yes | a basis that moves with the body, scalar-only trunk | at the input and output |

: Four routes to rigid-motion symmetry. How to read this: "exact" means the
property holds to roundoff for every input and every weight setting, the
sense of a contract in @sec-fidelity-columns. {#tbl-landscape-symmetry}

## Discretization: count-weighted and measure-weighted sums {#sec-landscape-discretization}

**Every aggregation in a network is a sum over tokens, and a sum over
sampled points converges to an integral against the sampling density, not
against the surface measure, unless each term carries its cell's
measure.** If the $N$ points are drawn with density $\rho$ on a surface
$\Gamma$, then
$\frac1N\sum_j f(y_j) \to \int_\Gamma f\,\rho\,dS$. That limit depends on
the mesher. Weighting each term by the cell measure,
$\sum_j w_j f(y_j)$ with $\sum_j w_j = |\Gamma|$, converges to
$\int_\Gamma f\,dS$ for any density: it is a quadrature rule. Under a
random, non-uniform draw the weights are Horvitz–Thompson weights, the
importance weights of Monte Carlo integration (@sec-sampling-laws).
@fig-isla-quadrature shows both sums on the airfoil under two meshers.

**Inside attention the fix is one term in the exponent.** Adding $\log w_j$
to the score of token $j$ turns the count-weighted softmax of
@eq-attention into a quadrature of the normalized kernel integral,

$$
\frac{w_j\, e^{s_j}}{\sum_l w_l\, e^{s_l}}
= \operatorname{softmax}_j\bigl(s_j + \log w_j\bigr),
$$

so splitting a cell into two halves leaves the output unchanged. Cao (2021)
reads attention without the softmax as a Petrov–Galerkin projection, a
quadrature on the grid. Berner et al. (2026) state the general principle for
attention in operator learning: quadrature weights in the normalization and
the aggregation, so that a layer has one limit under refinement. Transolver's slice states
$\sum_i a_{is} h_i / \sum_i a_{is}$ weight each token once. A slice state
then counts a cluster of small cells near a leading edge once per cell, so the mesher's refinement decides how much
that region weighs. ISLA's routing adds exactly the log-measure bias
(@sec-isla-quadrature). GLOBE multiplies each face's kernel by the face's
area (@eq-landscape-globe), so every sum it takes is a quadrature of a
boundary integral.

**"Resolution invariance" claims need to be read with their sampler.** A
neural operator is called discretization-invariant or
discretization-convergent when its layers converge to a continuum operator
as one family of discretizations is refined (Kovachki et al., 2023). That is
a statement about refinement of one mesher. It does not say that two
meshers with different cell densities give the same answer, and a
count-weighted layer converges to a different operator for each density,
as the plain means of @fig-isla-quadrature do. Models with a fixed
number of nearest neighbors change their stencil with resolution. A
fixed-radius graph does not, but it counts neighbors. A latent grid is
resolution-independent in its processor and depends on how points are
scattered onto it. The question to ask of any claim is which limit it
proves, and under which change of the sample it was measured. ISLA's
answer is in @sec-sampling-laws.

## Physics-informed losses, and why ISLA takes none {#sec-landscape-pinn}

**A physics-informed neural network penalizes the PDE residual of its
output. ISLA takes no such term, because the residual of the equations its
labels solve is not available to it and the metric scores the labels.** A
PINN represents one solution $u_\theta(x)$ as a network of the coordinates
and minimizes a weighted sum of the squared PDE residual at collocation
points, the boundary-condition residual and any data misfit, with the
derivatives taken by automatic differentiation (Raissi et al., 2019;
@sec-vs-bibliography). The loss is a soft constraint. Its optimization is
often ill-conditioned (Wang et al., 2021; Krishnapriyan et al., 2021), and
in its basic form one training solves one PDE instance. The
physics-informed neural operator adds residual terms to operator learning
(Li et al., 2024).

The book's industrial labels are time-averaged turbulent flows computed
with a turbulence closure or a scale-resolving model. The closure is an
empirical fit, and the residual a model could compute (the steady
Navier–Stokes equations with some closure) is not the residual the labels
satisfy. A penalty on it would pull predictions away from the labels the
metric scores. ISLA puts its physical structure in the architecture
instead: rigid-motion equivariance holds as an exact property of the map
(@sec-isla-contracts) and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature rule
by construction, where a penalty would hold such properties only
approximately.
AB-UPT takes a third road for one constraint: it predicts the vorticity as a
curl, so the output is divergence-free by construction, a hard constraint in
the output basis.

## A taxonomy {#sec-landscape-taxonomy}

**The families differ along five axes: what they read, whether they are
exactly equivariant to rigid motions, whether their sums are quadratures,
whether they answer at arbitrary interior points, and whether they reach
the $10^5$ to $10^7$ points of industrial meshes.** @tbl-landscape-taxonomy
places each family as it is published. A "no" in the equivariance or
quadrature column describes the construction, not the behavior: such a
model can learn the property approximately from data, and @sec-invariances
measures how well the two baselines of this book do.

| family (example) | input representation | exact rigid-motion equivariance | measure-weighted aggregation | interior queries | $10^5$–$10^7$ points |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| graph networks (MeshGraphNets, MP-PDE) | mesh graph, relative positions on edges | translations only | not by construction: sums over neighbors | at mesh nodes | with partitioning or graph hierarchies |
| equivariant graph networks (EGNN; tensor field networks, e3nn) | point graph, relative vectors | yes | not by construction | at graph nodes | costly at high tensor order |
| Fourier neural operators (FNO, Geo-FNO) | regular grid, or a learned map onto one | no (translations of a periodic grid) | uniform quadrature on the grid | at grid nodes, by interpolation | limited by the 3-D grid |
| GINO | point cloud and signed distance, carried onto a latent grid | no | converges under refinement, as published | yes | yes, as published |
| DeepONet | input at fixed sensors; query coordinates | no | not applicable: fixed sensors | yes, each point independent | in the trunk; the branch needs fixed sensors |
| latent tokens (Perceiver IO, UPT, AB-UPT) | point sets, cross-attended to latents or anchors | no | not by construction | yes, by cross-attention | yes; AB-UPT reports $1.5 \times 10^8$ cells |
| equivariant latent tokens (AB-GATr) | point sets in geometric algebra | yes | not by construction | yes | yes, at 2 to 11 times AB-UPT's training time |
| slice attention (Transolver, Transolver++, Transolver-3) | point set, raw coordinates | no | no: Transolver counts each token once | as tokens of the input set | yes, linear in $N$ |
| GeoTransolver | point set, raw coordinates, ball-query geometry encoding, global context | no | no: counts each token once | as tokens, with the signed distance | yes, linear in $N$ |
| boundary-integral kernels (GLOBE) | boundary faces by boundary-condition type (centroid, normal, area, data), no connectivity; reference lengths | yes, rotations, translations and reflections in the kernel; at a finite opening angle a rotation regroups its tree, whose boxes are aligned with the dataset's axes | yes: each face's kernel times its area | yes, at arbitrary points; its dual-tree traversal builds a tree over the prediction points, so at a finite opening angle a point's far-field list can depend on the other points requested | $N \log N$ with a Barnes–Hut tree in its PhysicsNeMo code; published dense, $N^2$, on two-dimensional airfoils |
| physics-informed networks (PINN) | coordinates of one instance | no | not applicable | yes | one instance per training |
| **ISLA** | boundary cells with their measure; invariants against slice anchors | **yes**, rotations, translations and reflections (@sec-isla-contracts); ISLA-DTT's tree read up to ties of its canonical frame (@sec-arch-tree-read) | **yes**: a log-measure bias in the routing | **yes**, as interacting or read-only prediction points | **yes**, linear in $N$; 200,000 cells per case in this book |

: The families of neural PDE surrogates against the five properties that
matter for steady boundary-driven problems, each as constructed in the
cited papers (@sec-vs-bibliography) and, for ISLA and GLOBE's tree, in
the PhysicsNeMo code. How to read
this: a row says what the architecture guarantees by construction, not how
accurate it is; accuracy is the subject of @sec-standing. {#tbl-landscape-taxonomy}

## The two gaps ISLA fills {#sec-landscape-gaps}

**ISLA draws on the best parts of GLOBE and Transolver. The scalable
slice and latent-token transformers pool by token count and take
raw coordinates; ISLA fills those two gaps by combining GLOBE's
principles with Transolver's slice attention in one transformer.** No
published slice or latent-token transformer at industrial scale is exactly
equivariant to rigid motions without typed features in every layer, and
none weights its aggregation by the measure the cells stand for, so their
predictions depend on the pose of the body and on the mesher's cell
density. From GLOBE (@sec-landscape-globe), ISLA takes the boundary as the
input, the rigid-motion symmetry built into the architecture, sums over
the boundary that are quadratures against the cells' measure, so that the
prediction is consistent under remeshing, and dimensionless geometry.
From Transolver (@sec-landscape-slice), it takes slice attention: a
learned soft partition that couples every point globally at a cost linear
in $N$. ISLA is not either architecture with a tweak: GLOBE couples
through a kernel per face–target pair, Transolver's slices see raw
coordinates and count tokens, and ISLA's slices are built on GLOBE's
principles. Every sum over the boundary is a quadrature rule. Positions
enter only as invariants of a token against the slices' own anchors, in
units of a length computed from the boundary. Vector
and tensor outputs are rebuilt at the end from a basis that moves with the
body. The trunk between those edges is an ordinary scalar transformer of
pre-LN blocks. How each of these works, on the same airfoil, is
@sec-isla.
